name: Amsterdam
tagline: Golden Age canals, gabled houses and easy sophistication.
whenBlurb: April to June for long light and the tulips, September for calm and mild days. Avoid the grey, wet, dark November-to-February stretch.

ourTake.lede: Amsterdam rewards slowness and punishes the checklist. Base yourself in the canal belt, walk or cycle everywhere, and give the big museums their first opening hour rather than the crowded middle of the day. The Jordaan and the quieter southern canals are where the city actually lives; the Red Light District and the coffee-shop trail are what everyone else came for, and you can happily skip both.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a walkable, cultured European city of canals and world-class museums taken at an unhurried pace.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing sun, beaches, or dramatic landscape; Amsterdam is a compact, urban, weather-dependent city.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: De L'Europe Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring, on the Amstel, by Muntplein
credentials: MICHELIN Three Keys (2025, the Netherlands' highest)
The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The city's original grand dame, on the Amstel since 1896, a classic European grand hotel, family-owned and freshly renovated.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Amsterdam
items.description: Six adjoining 17th-century canal mansions on the Herengracht, the only Forbes Five-Star hotel in the Netherlands, with a garden courtyard rare for the centre.

items.name: Rosewood Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring, former Palace of Justice, Prinsengracht
items.description: Rosewood's first Dutch house, in the 1665 former Palace of Justice on the Prinsengracht, 134 rooms, an Asaya spa and a 12-metre pool.

items.name: Conservatorium Hotel
items.area: Oud-Zuid, Museum Quarter, facing the Rijksmuseum side
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A former music conservatory turned soaring glass-roofed design hotel, opposite Museumplein, the city's most architectural luxury stay.

items.name: Hotel Okura Amsterdam
items.area: De Pijp, south of the centre
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A serene Japanese-run grand hotel with the city's greatest concentration of stars under one roof, three MICHELIN stars across its restaurants.

items.name: Anantara Grand Hotel Krasnapolsky Amsterdam
items.description: An 1865 landmark on Dam Square, reborn under Anantara, grand scale, a famous glass-roofed Winter Garden, and a Michelin kitchen within.

items.name: The Dylan Amsterdam
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: An intimate canal-house hotel on the Keizersgracht around a hidden courtyard, home to one of the city's two-star kitchens.

items.name: Pulitzer Amsterdam
items.description: Twenty-five interlinked 17th- and 18th-century canal houses between two canals, a whole block of the Grachtengordel turned into one characterful hotel.

items.name: Hotel TwentySeven
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A jewel-box, all-suite hotel of just sixteen suites on Dam Square, intensely private, with a one-star kitchen on the top floor.

items.name: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Maurits at the Park
items.area: Centre, by the Hortus Botanicus / Artis
items.description: A restored 19th-century mansion by the botanical garden, a polished, art-filled boutique house on the calmer eastern edge of the centre.

items.name: Tivoli Doelen Amsterdam
items.area: Canal Ring, on the Amstel, by Muntplein
items.description: One of the city's oldest hotel sites on the Amstel, reborn as a contemporary Tivoli, a classic Dutch address with fresh polish.

items.name: Rijksmuseum
items.description: The nation's treasure house, built for the Dutch Golden Age: Rembrandt's colossal Night Watch, Vermeer's quiet interiors, Delftware and ship models across eighty galleries. A private early-access tour before the doors open lets a family stand alone with the great canvases; the garden and the airy atrium café make an easy pause for younger children.

items.name: Van Gogh Museum
items.description: The largest Van Gogh collection on earth, roughly 200 paintings and 500 drawings hung to trace his life from Nuenen to Auvers, Sunflowers, Almond Blossom, The Bedroom in one place. Book a timed slot and go at opening; the multimedia guide is a gentle way to keep teenagers engaged.

items.name: Anne Frank House
items.description: The canal-side house on the Prinsengracht where Anne Frank, her family and four others hid for two years behind a bookcase, and where she wrote the diary. Tickets are timed and sell out weeks ahead, book the moment they release. A quiet, sobering hour that older children carry with them; the annex is steep and unsuitable for very young ones.

items.name: Stedelijk Museum
items.description: The Netherlands' museum of modern and contemporary art, from Malevich, Mondrian and Matisse through Warhol and Dutch design, in the landmark 'bathtub' extension on Museumplein. A natural third stop once the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh are done, and rarely as crowded.

items.name: The Canal Ring (Grachtengordel)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Seventeenth-century canal ring
items.description: The seventeenth-century belt of three grand canals, Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht, lined with gabled merchant houses, hump-backed bridges and houseboats. Simply wander the towpaths at golden hour; the 'Golden Bend' on the Herengracht holds the grandest of the old mansions.

items.name: Private canal cruise
items.description: See the city the way it was meant to be seen, from the water. A chartered open saloon boat with a skipper glides under the low bridges of the canal belt at dusk; arrange a private vessel with your own catering and a discreet crew rather than the packed public boats. The most relaxed way for multiple generations to take in the city together.

items.name: Jordaan
items.description: The former working-class quarter turned Amsterdam's most charming neighbourhood: narrow lanes, hidden courtyards (hofjes), independent galleries, brown cafés and antique shops along the Elandsgracht. Best enjoyed slowly on foot with no fixed plan, stopping wherever the window looks good.

items.name: The Nine Streets (De Negen Straatjes)
items.description: Nine little cross-streets threading between the main canals, packed with concept boutiques, vintage dealers, jewellers and specialist cafés, the best browsing in the old city. Compact enough to cover in an afternoon, with plenty of veg-friendly cafés and patisseries for a break.

items.name: De Pijp
items.description: Amsterdam's most vibrant food-and-drink district, built around the Albert Cuyp market and Sarphatipark. Bakeries, wine bars, and an unusually deep bench of Indian, Surinamese, Middle Eastern and vegetarian kitchens make it the easy choice when the family wants variety at dinner.

items.name: Albert Cuyp Market
items.description: The largest open-air market in the Netherlands, running since 1905 with 260-odd stalls of cheese, flowers, fabric, street food and stroopwafels pressed fresh. A lively morning stroll; watch the pockets and go early before the crowds thicken.

items.name: Amsterdam-Noord & NDSM Wharf
items.description: A two-minute free ferry across the IJ from Centraal delivers you to the city's creative frontier, a former shipyard of street-art hangars, design studios, waterfront restaurants and flea markets. A refreshing half-day away from the tourist core.

items.name: A'DAM Lookout
items.description: The highest public viewpoint in central Amsterdam, atop the 100-metre A'DAM Tower, with a 360-degree skydeck and 'Over the Edge', Europe's highest swing, out over the water. Cap it at the revolving Moon restaurant or the rooftop bar; the thrill-swing is a hit with teenagers.

items.name: EYE Filmmuseum
items.description: A sculptural white building on the northern bank of the IJ devoted to cinema, exhibitions, restored classics, and a waterfront terrace with one of the best views back across the water to the old city. Reachable on the same free ferry as A'DAM Lookout.

items.name: Vondelpark
items.description: Amsterdam's great green lung, opened in 1865: 47 hectares of ponds, lawns, rose garden and an open-air theatre, minutes from the museums. Rent bikes for the family, picnic on the grass, or take an early-morning run before the galleries open.

items.name: Hortus Botanicus
items.description: One of the world's oldest botanical gardens, laid out in 1638 as a physic garden for the city's doctors, with a butterfly house, a three-climate palm glasshouse and an ancient cycad collection among the finest in Europe. A calm, shaded green pause and lovely with children.

items.name: Begijnhof
items.description: A hushed medieval courtyard of almshouses hidden behind an unmarked door off the Spui, home to one of the city's oldest wooden houses and a clandestine chapel. Free, tranquil and easily missed, a moment of stillness a step off the busiest streets.

items.name: Museum Van Loon
items.description: A perfectly preserved patrician canal house on the Keizersgracht, still furnished as the Van Loon family (co-founders of the Dutch East India Company) kept it, with a formal French garden and coach house behind. An intimate, uncrowded glimpse of how the merchant elite actually lived.

items.name: Museum Willet-Holthuysen
items.description: The only fully furnished Amsterdam canal house open daily, a lavish Herengracht mansion redone in Louis XIV style with a rare surviving eighteenth-century garden. A quick, elegant complement to Museum Van Loon just around the corner.

items.name: Rembrandt House Museum
items.description: The house on the Jodenbreestraat where Rembrandt lived and worked for nearly twenty years at the height of his fame, reconstructed with his studio, cabinet of curiosities and printing press, with live etching demonstrations. A vivid, human counterpoint to seeing his masterworks at the Rijksmuseum.

items.name: Moco Museum
items.description: A townhouse on Museumplein showing crowd-pleasing modern and street art, Banksy, Basquiat, Warhol, KAWS, Haring, plus immersive digital rooms. Fast, fun and photogenic; the natural pick when the family wants contemporary energy between the old masters.

items.name: Royal Palace of Amsterdam
items.description: The seventeenth-century town hall on Dam Square, built to trumpet Amsterdam's Golden Age wealth and now one of the King's official palaces, marble halls, Empire furniture and a grand Citizens' Hall mapped with the heavens. Open to the public when no state functions are on; check the calendar first.

items.name: Nieuwe Kerk
items.description: The late-Gothic 'New Church' beside the Royal Palace, no longer a parish church but the setting for royal coronations and weddings and now a hall for major art and photography exhibitions. Worth stepping in to see what is showing beneath the soaring vaults.

items.name: Oude Kerk
items.description: The oldest building in Amsterdam, a 1300s church with a painted wooden ceiling and Rembrandt's wife buried beneath the floor, now doubling as a bold contemporary-art space in the heart of the old quarter. An arresting collision of the medieval and the modern.

items.name: Westerkerk
items.description: The tallest church tower in the city, finished in 1638, standing over the Prinsengracht beside the Anne Frank House, climb the Westertoren on a guided ascent for a rooftop panorama of the canal belt. Rembrandt is buried here in an unmarked grave.

items.name: Concertgebouw
items.description: A concert hall of near-mythic acoustics, ranked with Vienna's Musikverein and Boston's Symphony Hall, home to the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra since 1888. Book ahead for an evening concert, or catch the free Wednesday lunchtime rehearsal-concert, a cultured, dress-up night out.

items.name: Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder (Our Lord in the Attic)
items.description: A complete Catholic church hidden in the attic of a seventeenth-century canal house, built when public Catholic worship was banned, the second-oldest museum in Amsterdam and utterly unexpected. A remarkable, little-known secret in the heart of the old town.

items.name: Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga)
items.description: A vast, candlelit 1675 synagogue, among the grandest of its era, still lit only by hundreds of candles, with hidden treasure chambers open to visitors. Part of the Jewish Cultural Quarter alongside the Jewish Museum and National Holocaust Museum.

items.name: Bloemenmarkt (Floating Flower Market)
items.description: The world's only floating flower market, a line of stalls on barges along the Singel selling tulip bulbs, seeds and blooms since 1862. A quick, colourful stroll near the Munttoren, a pretty stop rather than a destination in itself.

items.name: Foam Photography Museum
items.description: A serious yet intimate photography museum in a Keizersgracht canal house, rotating its shows every few months across documentary, fashion and emerging talent. Small enough to enjoy in an hour and always current.

items.name: STRAAT Museum
items.description: A colossal shipyard warehouse at NDSM filled with more than 180 monumental street-art and graffiti works by 170-plus artists from around the world. Bold, immersive and a hit with older kids and teenagers; pairs naturally with the NDSM ferry outing.

items.name: H'ART Museum
items.description: A grand former almshouse on the Amstel, once the Hermitage Amsterdam, now hosting blockbuster loan exhibitions from major museums such as the British Museum and Smithsonian. A generously scaled space for a single, well-curated show.

items.name: NEMO Science Museum
items.description: A green copper Renzo Piano building shaped like a ship's prow, five floors of hands-on physics, chemistry and space experiments aimed squarely at children. The stepped rooftop is a free public terrace with a fine city view even if you skip the exhibits.

items.name: ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo
items.description: The oldest zoo in the Netherlands and one of the oldest still running in the world, set in a leafy nineteenth-century park with an aquarium, planetarium, butterfly pavilion and the Micropia microbe museum on site. A full, easy family day among fine old architecture.

items.name: Micropia
items.description: The only museum in the world devoted entirely to microbes, part of the ARTIS complex, living microorganisms under microscopes, a body-scanner that maps your own flora, and cheese-cultures explained. Genuinely novel and surprisingly gripping for curious teenagers.

items.name: Het Scheepvaartmuseum (National Maritime Museum)
items.description: The story of Dutch seafaring housed in a monumental 1656 admiralty warehouse, with a full-scale replica of the East India Company ship Amsterdam moored alongside to climb aboard. The replica ship makes it especially good with children.

items.name: Tropenmuseum
items.description: A grand ethnographic museum in a monumental building by the Oosterpark, telling the story of world cultures and the Dutch colonial past through immersive, thoughtfully reframed galleries. Of particular resonance for Indian visitors given the shared colonial and trade history.

items.name: Heineken Experience
items.description: An interactive tour of the original 1867 Heineken brewery on the Stadhouderskade, brewing history, a stable of dray horses, tastings and a rooftop bar. Slick and fun for a mixed group; the tasting can be skipped for younger travellers.

items.name: House of Bols
items.description: An interactive genever and cocktail experience opposite the Van Gogh Museum, telling the story of Lucas Bols, the world's oldest distilled-spirits brand (1575), and ending with a made-to-order cocktail at the mirror bar. A grown-ups' interlude between the galleries.

items.name: Gassan Diamonds
items.description: A working diamond polishing house in a former steam-powered factory, offering free guided tours of the cutting and grading process, and a discreet showroom for those who wish to buy. A natural fit for UHNI travellers with an eye for stones; private viewings can be arranged.

items.name: Cycling the city
items.description: Amsterdam runs on the bicycle, and there is no more authentic way to move through it, quiet residential canals, the Vondelpark, and the flat greenway north of the IJ. Hire from a reputable shop, or take a guided family ride to learn the etiquette before setting off alone.

items.name: Zaanse Schans (day trip)
items.description: An open-air village of working windmills, wooden houses, a clog workshop and a cheese farm on the Zaan river, about twenty minutes by train. The classic postcard-Holland half-day; go early to have the mills before the tour buses.

items.name: Haarlem (day trip)
items.description: A refined small city just fifteen minutes by train, with a splendid market square, the Grote Kerk, the Frans Hals Museum and the Teylers, the oldest museum in the country. A calmer, elegant alternative to a busy Amsterdam afternoon.

items.name: Utrecht (day trip)
items.description: A handsome canal city half an hour away, its wharves lined with waterside cafés below street level, the Dom Tower climbable for wide views, and Miffy's museum for younger children. Less crowded than Amsterdam and easy to reach by frequent train.

items.name: Keukenhof (seasonal day trip)
items.description: The world's grandest spring bulb garden, seven million tulips, daffodils and hyacinths in bloom across 32 hectares, open only from mid-March to mid-May. A dazzling seasonal excursion; a chauffeured car or helicopter avoids the peak crowds and coach queues.

items.name: Giethoorn (day trip)
items.description: The 'Venice of the North', a car-free village of thatched farmhouses linked only by canals and wooden footbridges, reached by whisper-quiet electric boat. About two hours out, best as a full-day escape, ideally with a private driver, for a wholly peaceful day on the water.

items.name: Spectrum
items.description: Sidney Schutte's precise, layered cooking in the Waldorf Astoria, two stars and one of the city's benchmark tasting tables.

items.name: Ciel Bleu
items.description: A two-star institution on the 23rd floor of the Okura, refined contemporary cooking with the finest dining view in the city.

items.name: Flore
items.area: Canal Ring, Nieuwe Doelenstraat, by the Amstel
items.description: Bas van Kranen's near-vegetarian, hyper-seasonal cooking, two stars and a Green Star, one of the most forward kitchens in the Netherlands.

items.name: Vinkeles
items.description: Two-star French cooking in an atmospheric 18th-century former bakery within The Dylan, one of the city's great romantic rooms.

items.name: Restaurant 212
items.description: An open-kitchen counter on the Amstel where you watch two-star cooking up close, theatrical, precise and personal.

items.name: RIJKS
items.description: A one-star kitchen inside the Rijksmuseum, locally sourced Dutch cooking beside the world's great Rembrandts.

items.name: The White Room
items.description: Refined cooking under an ornate 1885 ceiling on Dam Square, a one-star room of real grandeur inside the Krasnapolsky.

items.name: Bougainville
items.description: Tim Golsteijn's elegant one-star cooking with panoramic views over Dam Square, a jewel-box room above the square.

items.name: De Kas
items.description: A daily-changing menu grown in the restaurant's own 1926 greenhouse, the original farm-to-table Amsterdam, now with a star and a Green Star.

items.name: Bolenius
items.description: Vegetables and herbs from its own kitchen garden drive this one-star, Green-Star kitchen in the Zuidas, quietly one of the city's most sustainable tables.

items.name: Yamazato
items.description: Authentic Japanese kaiseki that earned a MICHELIN star, a rare traditional Japanese room outside Japan, inside the Okura.

items.name: Daalder
items.description: Relaxed but serious one-star cooking in the west of the city, casual fine dining that quietly punches above its room.

items.name: Wils
items.description: Live-fire, wood-fired cooking with a great wine list, a one-star grill that does open flame beautifully.

items.name: Sinne
items.description: A neighbourhood one-star in De Pijp doing refined French–Mediterranean menus at a friendlier price than the grand rooms.

items.name: MOS
items.area: Eastern Docklands, IJdok, on the IJ
items.description: A small one-star room on the IJ waterfront, precise French-and-international cooking with water on three sides.

items.name: De Juwelier
items.description: Richard van Oostenbrugge and Thomas Groot's Franco-inspired seafood room, a stylish, contemporary one-star on Utrechtsestraat.

items.name: Bistro de la Mer
items.description: A refined French seafood bistro that earned a star, classic technique, beautifully sourced fish, unfussy elegance.

items.name: Zoldering
items.description: An intimate one-star with a serious wine focus, considered French cooking in a small, personal room.

items.name: Freddy's Bar
items.area: Canal Ring, De L'Europe, on the Amstel
credentials: Inside De L'Europe, a MICHELIN Three-Key hotel
items.description: The clubby, panelled bar of the De L'Europe grand hotel, named for Freddy Heineken, and a classic Amsterdam institution.

items.name: Pulitzer's Bar
credentials: Inside the Pulitzer, a MICHELIN One-Key hotel
items.description: A stylish gentleman's-club-style bar across three rooms inside the Pulitzer, over fifty cocktails and real canal-house character.

items.name: Tales & Spirits
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A long-running Amsterdam favourite in an ancient building, an inventive, humour-filled list and warm, expert hospitality.

items.name: Door 74
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: The Netherlands' first true speakeasy, unmarked, reservation-only, and still one of the city's best cocktail rooms.

items.name: Flying Dutchmen Cocktails
items.area: Canal Ring, Singel, in the Odeon
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: Tess Posthumus and Timo Janse's bar in the 1662 Odeon, over 900 spirits, the biggest selection in the country, and a classics-first ethos.

items.name: Rosalia's Menagerie
items.area: De Wallen, on one of the oldest canals
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery
items.description: A temple to Dutch spirits in a townhouse in the Old Town, thought to hold the largest genever selection in the Netherlands.

items.name: Advocatuur
credentials: Inside Rosewood Amsterdam, a MICHELIN Two-Key hotel
items.description: The signature bar of Rosewood Amsterdam in the former Palace of Justice, a polished, contemporary drinking room in the city's newest grand hotel.

items.name: Twenty Third Bar
credentials: Alongside Ciel Bleu, a two-MICHELIN-star restaurant
items.description: A high, glass-walled bar beside Ciel Bleu on the 23rd floor of the Okura, the best skyline view for a drink in the city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Amsterdam, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at the Waldorf Astoria on the Herengracht, then the Rijksmuseum, guided, for the Vermeers and the Night Watch.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private saloon boat through the canal ring, the merchants' houses from the water.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Spectrum at the Waldorf, two Michelin stars, canal-side.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Van Gogh Museum from opening, the letters and the late fields.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Anne Frank House by timed entry, then the Jordaan's quiet courtyards and galleries.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Rijks or Bougainville, refined and rooted in the season.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A car to Delft for the old town, the Nieuwe Kerk, and the Royal Delft workshop.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Mauritshuis in The Hague for Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner back in Amsterdam at Ciel Bleu, high over the city.

items.name: Grachtengordel (Canal Belt)
items.description: The postcard heart; suits a first visit that wants to walk out of the door and into the Amsterdam of the imagination.

items.name: Jordaan
items.description: Former working-class lanes turned quietly chic; for those who prefer neighbourhood cafés and small galleries to landmarks.

items.name: Oud-Zuid (Old South)
items.description: Leafy, residential and moneyed, beside the museum quarter and Vondelpark; suits families and anyone wanting calm and space.

events.name: King's Day (Koningsdag)
events.note: The whole city turns orange and takes to the streets and canals for the country's biggest party; book rooms far ahead.

events.name: Amsterdam Light Festival
events.note: Illuminated artworks along the canals, best seen from a heated boat on a cold winter evening.

events.name: Tulip season and Keukenhof
events.note: The bulb fields and the gardens outside the city are at their peak; the single reason many travellers time spring here.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay along the Grachtengordel canal ring or in the Museum Quarter for calm and proximity; the city is understated rather than showy, so dress is relaxed, and private after-hours viewings at the major museums can be arranged.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Schiphol; a chauffeured car covers the 20-minute run into the canal belt, and the airport's own rail link is fast if preferred.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Walking is the joy of the old centre, complemented by a private car or a chartered saloon boat along the canals.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent everywhere; a KPN or Vodafone eSIM works well, and wifi is fast and widespread.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; the Dutch are a near-cashless society and cards work everywhere, so tipping is light, rounding up or a few percent.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: May-June brings tulip season's tail, long light and mild, dry-ish days; September is calm and golden. Avoid November-February for short, damp, grey days, and note April's tulip peak draws heavy crowds.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Nonstop from Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru in roughly 9-10 hours. KLM flies it most frequently with a solid World Business Class; Air India also serves it direct. Schiphol is compact and efficient, and KLM's Crown Lounge and single-terminal layout make onward European connections painless.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; very safe and orderly. Ordinary care against bicycle traffic and canal-side edges. Tap water is excellent and safe.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy; Jain and strict no-onion-garlic want advance notice. A strong Surinamese-Indian and Indian scene means good roti and thali houses; the city's fine-dining kitchens cater to vegetarians readily when briefed ahead.
